title: Azure DevOps Pricing: Plans and Costs Explained (2026)
summary: Azure DevOps pricing covers planning, code storage, building and testing tools across tiers. You'll see which plan matches your team size and budget.
body_markdown:
## Automating Azure DevOps events with Activepieces


Don't expect your Azure DevOps bill to drop because of Activepieces.


What it can do is take over the small manual jobs that otherwise eat your team's hours, such as telling people a build broke or copying a request into the right tracker, and its Free plan costs $0 for up to 5 users.


Put simply, Activepieces waits for something to happen in one system, then runs a set of steps in others, across 746 integrations in an MIT-licensed core.


Skip it and those steps fall to whoever notices first, which is usually the most expensive person in the room.


To announce events, Azure DevOps uses service hooks, which are outbound notifications it sends to a web address when something happens, such as a pipeline run finishing.


Activepieces gives that address a place to land and then runs a flow, meaning a chain of steps you set up once.


Its pricing page lists 1 credit per flow run, any number of steps, where Zapier bills per task and Make per module, and the Free plan includes 1,000 credits a month with unlimited flows, so an alert that fans out into five steps still counts as one run.


It can also call Azure DevOps directly through its API, the interface programs use to talk to it.


Follow the path in the picture below. A pipeline sends a service hook into an Activepieces flow, and the flow splits into a chat message and a work item in a separate tool, two branches that still cost 1 credit per run.


Take from it that one event can feed two places without anyone retyping it. What it leaves out is the setup, and what follows is where that effort goes.


### Azure DevOps pipeline failure alerts in chat


Nobody reads the failed-build emails Azure DevOps already sends. A flow can catch the failure and post it to the channel your team actually reads.


It puts the pipeline name, the branch and a link to the run in front of people while it's still fresh. Without it, a broken build can sit unnoticed until someone goes looking, and the delay is paid for in waiting developers.


You can also filter. The flow can post only failures on your main branch and stay quiet about experiments, so the channel stays worth reading.


### Creating work items from other tools


The reverse direction works too. When a request arrives in a tool outside Azure DevOps, such as a support desk or a form, a flow can call the Azure DevOps API.


It creates a work item, the tracked task or bug, with the details already filled in. That removes the copy-and-paste step where details get dropped.


Be clear about the limits. Activepieces doesn't change what Azure DevOps charges for parallel jobs ($40 a month per extra hosted job), Test Plans ($52 per user), Artifacts storage or licences, and it doesn't replace any of them.


It also adds a system you have to host or pay for and keep running, from $20 a month flat on the Plus plan or the self-hosted Community Edition under the MIT licence, so count that in your estimate before you count the saved hours.
